blocks.content: kubectl exec runs a command, or opens an interactive shell, inside an already-running Pod, the Kubernetes-level equivalent of docker exec, covered throughout the Docker course.
1. Live Debugging, Inside a Running Pod
blocks.text: 1. Live Debugging, Inside a Running Pod

blocks.content: When logs and describe alone are not enough, kubectl exec lets you get directly inside an already-running Pod, to inspect files, check configuration, or run diagnostic commands live.

blocks.alt: Direct, live access inside a Pod that is already up and running

blocks.content: 2. Conceptually the Same as docker exec
blocks.text: 2. Conceptually the Same as docker exec

blocks.content: This is exactly the same idea covered in the Docker Containers module, running an additional process inside a container that is already alive, Kubernetes simply extends the same concept to a Pod running somewhere in the cluster.

blocks.alt: The exact same underlying idea, extended from a single container to a cluster-wide Pod

blocks.content: Exactly as with kubectl logs, a Pod holding several containers requires -c to specify which one you actually want to enter, without it, the command has no way to know which container you mean.

blocks.alt: The same -c requirement, the moment a Pod holds more than one container

blocks.content: 4. What to Do Without a Shell
blocks.text: 4. What to Do Without a Shell

blocks.content: A distroless container, exactly the case covered in the Docker Performance module, has no shell to exec into at all, this is precisely what Ephemeral Containers, covered in the Pods module, exist to solve, attaching a separate debugging image temporarily instead.

blocks.alt: The exact case Ephemeral Containers, covered in the Pods module, were built to solve

blocks.content: Dropping into an interactive shell to check an environment variable, inspect a mounted config file, or manually test connectivity to another Service, are all common, practical uses of this command during live debugging.

blocks.alt: The practical, everyday reasons this command actually gets reached for

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: kubectl exec runs a command or shell inside an already-running Pod, conceptually the exact same idea as docker exec, covered throughout the Docker course.
A distroless container with no shell needs Ephemeral Containers instead, covered in the Pods module, exec alone cannot help without a shell to attach to.
